decision.explanation: By linearity, L{cos(2t)+2sin(t)} = L{cos(2t)}+2L{sin(t)} = s/(s²+4)+2/(s²+1), using ω=2 for cosine and ω=1 for sine.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ for $s>0.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+L{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{cos⁡2t+2sin⁡t}=L{cos⁡2t}+L{2sin⁡t}=L{cos⁡2t}+2L{sin⁡t}.

We are given that L{sin⁡ωt}=ωs2+ω2,s>0,L{cos⁡ωt}=ss2+ω2,s>0.

Therefore, we have the following: L{cos⁡2t}=ss2+4,s>0L{sin⁡t}=1s2+1,s>0

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is L{f(t)}=L{cos⁡2t}+2L{sin⁡t}=ss2+4+2⋅1s2+1=ss2+4+2s2+1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Combined Functions
content.problem:
Given that for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t}=\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ for $s>0.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+L{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4},\,s>0 \\ L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}+2L{\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+2\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4}+\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}$ for $s>3.$
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}} & =L{{e}^{3t}}+L{-{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

 
Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s+1},\,s>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\  & =\frac{(s+1)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{s+1-s+3}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{(s-3)(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)} where α and β are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{e3t−e−t}=L{e3t}+L{−e−t}=L{e3t}−L{e−t}.

Next, we recall the following result: L{ekt}=1s−k,s>k Therefore, we have the following: L{e3t}=1s−3,s>3L{e−t}=1s+1,s>−1

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is L{f(t)}=L{e3t}−L{e−t}=1s−3−1s+1=(s+1)−(s−3)(s−3)(s+1)=s+1−s+3(s−3)(s+1)=4(s−3)(s+1).

Finally, since L{e3t} is defined for s∈(3,∞) and L{e−t} is defined for s∈(−1,∞), we have that L{f(t)} is defined for (3,∞)∩(−1,∞)=(3,∞), that is, s>3.

content.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}$ for $s>3.$
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)}
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}-{e}^{-t}} & =L{{e}^{3t}}+L{-{e}^{-t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following result:

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k
$$

 
Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-t}} & =\frac{1}{s+1},\,s>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{3t}}-L{{e}^{-t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-3}-\frac{1}{s+1} \\  & =\frac{(s+1)-(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{s+1-s+3}{(s-3)(s+1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{(s-3)(s+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-1,\infty ),$ we have that $L{f(t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)+(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

content.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{kt}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that, by definition

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)=\frac{{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}}{2}.
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{3t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-3t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{kt}}=\frac{1}{s-k},\,s>k.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{1}{s-3},\,s>3 \\ L{{e}^{-3t}} & =\frac{1}{s+3},\,s>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{3t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-3}+\frac{1}{s+3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+3)+(s-3)}{(s-3)(s+3)}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}-9}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}-9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $L{{e}^{3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (3,\infty )$ and $L{{e}^{-3t}}$ is defined for $s\in (-3,\infty ),$ we have that $L{\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)}$ is defined for

$$
(3,\infty )\cap (-3,\infty )=(3,\infty ),
$$

that is, $s>3.$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the cosine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)=\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}+{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}+{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+5\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-5\text{i}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+5\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-5\text{i}}+\frac{1}{s+5\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+5\text{i})+(s-5\text{i})}{(s-5\text{i})(s+5\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+25}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+25},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

content.worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the cosine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)=\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}+{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}+{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-5\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+5\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{5\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-5\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-5\text{i}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+5\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-5\text{i}}+\frac{1}{s+5\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+5\text{i})+(s-5\text{i})}{(s-5\text{i})(s+5\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+25}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+25},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$
